source_reference: G. Lan, First-Order and Stochastic Optimization Methods for Machine Learning, Springer 2020, Section 6.1.2.1 (Theorem 6.3)

problem.description: Unconstrained stochastic zeroth-order optimization with f represented as an expectation.

assumptions.name: Convex_problem_optional
assumptions.math: \text{problem (6.1.47) is convex with an optimal solution }x^*

initialization.math: \text{Input: Initial point }x_1,\text{ iteration limit }N,\text{ stepsizes }\{\gamma_k\}_{k\ge 1},\text{ probability mass function }P_R(\cdot)\text{ supported on }\{1,\ldots,N\}.\ \text{Step 0. Let }R\text{ be a random variable with probability mass function }P_R.

parameters.name: Gaussian_direction_distribution
parameters.math: \text{Let }u\text{ be n-dimensional standard Gaussian random vector and }\mu>0\text{ be the smoothing parameter.}

main_theorem.statement_math: \text{Suppose that the stepsizes }\{\gamma_k\}\text{ and the probability mass function }P_R(\cdot)\text{ in the RSGF method are chosen such that }\gamma_k<1/[2(n+4)L]\text{ and }P_R(k):=\mathrm{Prob}\{R=k\}=\frac{\gamma_k-2L(n+4)\gamma_k^2}{\sum_{k=1}^N[\gamma_k-2L(n+4)\gamma_k^2]},\ k=1,\ldots,N.\ \text{Then, under Assumptions 13 and 15, (a) for any }N\ge 1,\ \frac{1}{L}\mathrm{E}[\|\nabla f(x_R)\|^2]\le \frac{1}{\sum_{k=1}^N[\gamma_k-2L(n+4)\gamma_k^2]}\left(D_f^2+2\mu^2(n+4)\left[1+L(n+4)^2\sum_{k=1}^N(\gamma_k/4+L\gamma_k^2)\right]+2(n+4)\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^N\gamma_k^2\right),\ \text{where the expectation is taken with respect to }R,\xi_{[N]},\text{ and }u_{[N]},\text{ and }D_f\text{ is defined in (6.1.13);}\ \text{(b) if, in addition, problem (6.1.47) is convex with an optimal solution }x^*,\text{ then, for any }N\ge 1,\ \mathrm{E}[f(x_R)-f^*]\le \frac{1}{2\sum_{k=1}^N[\gamma_k-2(n+4)L\gamma_k^2]}\left(D_X^2+2\mu^2L(n+4)\sum_{k=1}^N[\gamma_k+L(n+4)^2\gamma_k^2]+2(n+4)\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^N\gamma_k^2\right),\ \text{where the expectation is taken with respect to }R,\xi_{[N]},\text{ and }u_{[N]},\text{ and }D_X\text{ is defined in (6.1.15).}
main_theorem.rate: For the constant stepsize and smoothing choices in Corollary 6.3, the iteration complexity for an expected epsilon-stationary point is O(n/epsilon^2).
main_theorem.measure: Expected squared gradient norm for the nonconvex case; expected optimality gap for the convex case.

proof.description: Introduce the combined random variable and the smoothed-gradient residual used throughout the proof.
proof.ref: Proof of Theorem 6.3, definitions before (6.1.64)
proof.math: \zeta_k\equiv(\xi_k,u_k),\ k\ge 1,\ \zeta_{[N]}:=(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_N),\ \mathrm{E}_{\zeta_{[N]}}\text{ denote the expectation w.r.t. }\zeta_{[N]},\ \Delta_k\equiv G_\mu(x_k,\xi_k,u_k)-\nabla f^\mu(x_k)\equiv G_\mu(x_k,\zeta_k)-\nabla f^\mu(x_k),\ k\ge 1.

The PDF says this second inequality follows from (6.1.20) and convexity of f^\mu, but it does not print a coefficient-level derivation of the replacement of the positive term 2(n+4)\sum_k\gamma_k^2 E[\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2] by 2(n+4)L\sum_k\gamma_k^2 E[f(x_k)-f^*]; this step records that printed transition as asserted by the source rather than deriving it from (6.1.3).

proof.description: Derive the prerequisite bridge needed for the last printed convex inequality: applying the pointwise smoothing bound (6.1.51) at x_k and at x^*, and using that x^* is an optimal solution so f(x^*)=f^*, gives f^\mu(x_k)-f^\mu(x^*) >= f(x_k)-f^*-\mu^2Ln. This is the source-backed bridge from f^\mu(x^*) to f^*; the paper cites (6.1.57) for the displayed transition, but (6.1.57) itself compares against f^{\mu,*}, not f^\mu(x^*).
